anchors.fact: Born in 1955 in Tullibody, Scotland, near the Cambus distillery where his father worked; he started there at 17, in 1973 (Oxford Companion, NICHOL, pdf 1388). In his telling, you got a job there if your father or uncle already had one (*Difford's Guide*, 2015).
anchors.meaning: The gift grew inside the people he came from. It was never a way out.

anchors.fact: When Cambus closed in 1993 he went to Cameronbridge in Fife, making liquid carbon dioxide, then grain whisky and neutral grain spirit from 1996 (Oxford pdf 1388). His own words on that spirit: hardly appreciated, because it "tastes of nothing and smells of nothing" (*The Spirits Business*, 2013).
anchors.meaning: Years making the part of the drink nobody notices. Talent in a place you'd never expect to find it.
anchors.speaksTo: appearances can sometimes be deceptive; fear of Exclusion

anchors.fact: In 2005 he joined the team making gin and vodka at Cameronbridge, and within a year he was Tanqueray's master distiller (Oxford pdf 1388). Tanqueray has been made in Scotland since 1998 (Oxford pdf 1986), and in his time it was made at Cameronbridge (*Difford's Guide*; the Gin Guild; his own "two stills for Tanqueray", 2013).
anchors.meaning: The gift came out where he already stood. He didn't have to leave to be found.

anchors.fact: He's credited with developing the Rangpur (2007), producing the Old Tom (2014) and the Bloomsbury (2015), and with maintaining the London Dry (Oxford pdf 1388). In his words, he made "a few other gins for Tanqueray" (*Difford's Guide*, 2015).
anchors.meaning: The talent was real, and it was his.

anchors.fact: Oxford calls him a "passionate, even irascible" advocate of the idea that big distilleries don't automatically make worse spirit (pdf 1388).
anchors.meaning: He stood up for the place everyone looked down on, and for the people who worked there.

anchors.fact: He called the master distiller's job "a testament to my father" (*The Spirits Business*, 2013). He lived some forty years in Alloa, a couple of miles from where he was born (*Difford's Guide*, 2015).
anchors.meaning: He kept both: the gift, and the people he came from.

anchors.fact: In May 2015, as he retired, the Gin Guild gave him its Lifetime Achievement Award. He said it was "completely unexpected" and that his father would have been proud (the Gin Guild).
anchors.meaning: The moment the room sees it, and he thinks first of home.

cocktail.closingLine: Make it where everyone is, not in the other room. Someone will ask about the finish.
cocktail.glassware: plain kitchen tumbler (about 250 ml), three or four ordinary ice cubes from the freezer tray
method: Make the syrup: put the sugar, water and liquorice root in a small pan and bring it just to a simmer, stirring until the sugar is gone. Let it simmer gently for 5 minutes, then take it off the heat and leave it for 30 minutes. Strain out the root and let the syrup cool.
Put the syrup and the bitters in a plain tumbler first, then pour in the gin.
Add three or four ordinary ice cubes and stir for about 20 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels cold. Then stop: the cubes keep melting as you drink.
cocktail.name: Right Here

recipe.note: the gin Tom Nichol looked after; or any juniper-led London dry gin, 40% to 47%. If your bottle says 47% or more, use 50 ml
brings forward the hint of liquorice the gin is said to have already

recipe.item: *for the syrup:* 100 g white sugar, 100 ml water, 5 g dried liquorice root (about two finger-length pieces), chopped or snapped small
recipe.note: makes about 160 ml; keeps two weeks in a closed jar in the fridge. Dried liquorice root is sold in health-food and tea shops. Check the pack for a nut warning. Liquorice sweets won't do: they aren't the root

cocktail.tagline: You thought you had to choose. You never did.

reading.epigraph: Four plants flavour this gin, they say. The last you taste comes first here.
whoYouAre: There's something you're good at that doesn't match the picture people have of you. A cake nobody believed you'd made. A song you only sing in the car. A drawing on the back of a work envelope. When someone finds out and says "you never said", you laugh and change the subject. Part of you has always believed you had to pick: be good at it, or stay one of them.

The truth is, you want both. And you've got one thing wrong: when it shows, nobody you love thinks you've got above yourself. They're proud it's one of theirs who did it. That's your gift to them, more than the cake or the song: it shows them what someone like them can do.
yours: Tom Nichol grew up in Tullibody, in Scotland, near the distillery where his father worked. At seventeen he was dragged into it, screaming and shouting, he says: his father had set up the interview. For over thirty years he worked in whisky and in jobs nobody outside a distillery hears about, including liquid carbon dioxide and plain grain spirit. It gets little thanks, he said, because it tastes of nothing and smells of nothing.

In 2005 he moved to the gin team at the same distillery, where Tanqueray was made. Within a year he was Tanqueray's master distiller, in charge of the gin itself. He's credited with new Tanqueray gins of his own, and with keeping the everyday one as it should be. When he retired in 2015, the gin trade's guild gave him a lifetime award. He called it completely unexpected, and said his father would have been very proud of him.

He'd lived forty years by then a couple of miles from where he was born, and he argued one idea hard, sometimes short-temperedly: a big distillery doesn't have to make worse spirit than a small one. I like to think you'd recognise that: the talent turned up right where life had put him, and once it was noticed, he didn't leave the place behind; he stood up for it.

The cocktail I've made for you is a gin Old-Fashioned, the classic of spirit, sugar and bitters, built in an ordinary tumbler over ice from the freezer tray. The gin is Tanqueray London Dry, with nothing to cover it. It's said to be made with only four plants: juniper, coriander, angelica and liquorice, the hint that comes at the finish. So the sugar comes as a liquorice root syrup, in honour of a talent that was in that distillery long before anyone named it. The liquorice is the gin's own, they say: it only brings forward what was already there.

So show it to the people who knew you first, before strangers. Make the cake for your own table. Sing with the window down on the way to your family's. Nobody will think you've changed. You'll find out you never had to choose, and they'll get to be proud of something that's theirs too.
